title: How nerves connect sensation, action and regulation
intro: The nervous system receives information, processes it and coordinates responses. It includes conscious movement and automatic regulation. Numbness, weakness and pain can arise at different levels, so a symptom map is not a diagnosis.

sections.heading: Central and peripheral
paragraphs: The brain and spinal cord form the central system. Peripheral nerves connect them with skin, muscles and organs; damage to a nerve differs from damage in the spinal cord or brain.

sections.heading: Passing messages
paragraphs: Neurons use electrical impulses and chemical messengers. Myelin helps many fibers conduct efficiently. Supporting cells and adequate blood supply are also essential, not just the nerve cells themselves.

sections.heading: Action and reflexes
paragraphs: Motor signals activate muscles; sensory signals report conditions. Some reflex circuits respond through the spinal cord before conscious interpretation, helping withdraw from danger without deliberate planning.

sections.heading: Automatic control
paragraphs: Autonomic pathways regulate functions such as heart rate, digestion and sweating. Sympathetic and parasympathetic activity balance changing demands; symptoms are not proof of a single system being permanently switched on.

sections.heading: Assessment and urgency
paragraphs: An examination may assess power, sensation and reflexes, with targeted tests if needed. Sudden weakness or speech change, or new bladder difficulty with saddle numbness and back symptoms, requires urgent help.

A diagram explains typical structure, not the cause of an individual symptom. Before a consultation, note when a change began, what brings it on and how it affects daily activities. Bring previous results and ask how the findings fit together.

examples.text: In this hypothetical example, Mira describes where numbness starts and which tasks are difficult, helping distinguish possible nerve pathways rather than diagnosing from an internet drawing.

examples.title: Another practical example
